568.title: The second paragraph (Deuteronomy 11:13–21)
568.hook: what we do affects the rain and the harvest
568.howItsDone: The second paragraph of the Shema, Deuteronomy 11:13–21, is said morning and evening after the first; in some Reform prayer books it is optional or replaced, while Orthodox and Conservative prayer books include it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baruch shem, the whispered line after the Shema. Your line was some words are whispered. Today, the Shema keeps going, into a paragraph about rain.

The Shema doesn't stop at its first line, or at the paragraph after it: love the LORD your God with all your heart, teach these words to your children, write them on your doorposts. It has three paragraphs. The second comes from later in Deuteronomy, and it sounds like a farmer's almanac with a warning label. Rain in its season. Grass for the cattle. Then a hard turn: what the people do reaches the sky and the soil.
screen: `THE SHEMA HAS THREE PARAGRAPHS.` → `A FARMER'S ALMANAC.` → `WITH A WARNING LABEL.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the old Jewish translation: "And it shall come to pass, if ye shall hearken diligently unto My commandments which I command you this day, to love the LORD your God, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." If you do, then rain: "the former rain and the latter rain," grain and wine and oil, grass for your animals. If your heart turns away to other gods, the sky closes, the land gives no harvest, and you are lost from the good land. Then it repeats the commands from the first paragraph: these words on your heart, on your hand, on your doorposts, taught to your children. Three things stand out. First, the grammar. The first paragraph speaks to you, singular. This one speaks mostly to you, plural: a whole community, together. Second, the order. The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, explains why this paragraph comes second: first a person accepts the kingdom of heaven, and only then the yoke of the commandments. Third, the phrase serve him with all your heart. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, asks: what is service of the heart? And answers: prayer. The phrase you met a few weeks ago, avodah shebalev, comes from here. The idea that rain answers obedience has troubled readers, and Jewish movements have handled it differently. The classic Reform prayer book left this paragraph out. Orthodox and Conservative prayer books keep it, and newer Reform prayer books often offer it again. Some readers today hear it simply: what we do, together, reaches the land.

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you did yesterday, a meal you cooked, something you threw away, a word said in anger or in kindness, and follow it outward. Whose rain grew the food, where did the trash go, who carried that word home? Follow it two or three steps, slowly.
Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart — the Talmud's name for prayer, drawn from the Shema's second paragraph: serve Him with all your heart.
Your line: what we do matters. And prayer, the rabbis say, is service of the heart. Day five hundred sixty-eight, done.

569.title: The third paragraph (Numbers 15:37–41)
569.hook: the fringes, and the Exodus remembered morning and night
569.howItsDone: The third paragraph of the Shema, Numbers 15:37–41, is said morning and evening; in the morning, many people holding their tzitzit kiss them each time the word is said and look at them while reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, avodah shebalev, and the second paragraph's rain and harvest. Your line was what we do matters. Today, the Shema's last paragraph.

People tie strings around fingers. They write on the backs of their hands, set a photo as the lock screen, keep a beach stone in a pocket. Humans are forgetful, and know it, so they hang reminders on their bodies. The third paragraph of the Shema is about exactly that: a reminder you wear. And in many synagogues, while it's read, people lift the fringes they gathered earlier and kiss them, again and again, at one particular word.
screen: `A STRING AROUND A FINGER.` → `REMINDERS WE WEAR.` → `KISSING THE FRINGES.`

segments.voice: The paragraph comes from the Book of Numbers. God tells Moses to have the people make tzitzit, fringes, on the corners of their garments, with a thread of blue in each. The reason is given right there. In the old Jewish translation: "that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them." Look, remember, do. Then a warning: not to go wandering after your own heart and your own eyes. The eyes see things and the heart wants them; the fringes are a counterweight you can see. The word tzitzit appears three times in the paragraph, and many people kiss the fringes at each one. The blue thread, tekhelet, came from a dye whose source was lost for many centuries; some people today wear blue threads again from a dye they believe is the ancient one, while others wear all white. The paragraph ends with the Exodus: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. That's why it's said at night too, even though fringes are a daytime commandment. The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, records an old argument: must the Exodus be remembered at night? Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says he couldn't win the point until Ben Zoma read a verse: all the days of your life. The days of your life means the days. All the days includes the nights. So the Exodus is remembered twice a day, morning and evening.

segments.voice: Find an object near you that carries a memory, a ring, a photo, a book someone gave you, a child's drawing, and hold it. Let it remind you who gave it and what it asks of you; then, if it feels right, kiss it or press it to your heart, the way people kiss the fringes. Look, remember, do.
Tzitzit. Fringes, tied to the four corners of a garment — look at them, the Torah says, and remember all the commandments, and do them.
Your line: remember twice a day. All the days of your life includes the nights. Until tomorrow.

570.title: True and firm
570.hook: after the Shema comes "true", affirming what was said
570.carry: more than a dozen words, all saying yes
570.howItsDone: Right after the last words of the Shema, the prayer leader and congregation say emet, joining it without a pause, and the morning blessing Emet v'Yatziv follows; in the evening the parallel blessing is Emet ve'Emunah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third paragraph: tzitzit, the fringes, and the Exodus. Your line was remember twice a day. Today, the word that comes the instant the Shema ends.

A friend has just told you something big. When they finish, there's a beat of silence, and then you say: that's true. I believe you. It changes what just happened. Their words are no longer only theirs; you've signed your name next to them. The Shema has just finished, three paragraphs from Deuteronomy and Numbers. And before anyone takes a breath, the prayer book puts one word right on its heels, so close there isn't supposed to be a pause at all. True.
screen: `A FRIEND TELLS YOU SOMETHING BIG.` → `THAT'S TRUE.` → `NO PAUSE AT ALL.`

segments.voice: The Shema ends: I am the LORD your God. The next word is emet, true. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, says not to pause between them. Tradition finds the pairing in the prophet Jeremiah. In the old Jewish translation: "But the LORD God is the true God." So the end of the Shema and the first word after it make one sentence: the LORD your God is true. Then the morning blessing carries on: emet v'yatziv, true and firm. And it doesn't stop at two. True and firm, established and lasting, right and faithful, beloved and cherished, delightful and pleasant, awesome and mighty, well-ordered and accepted, good and beautiful, is this word to us forever. More than a dozen words, piled up, all saying yes. It's a very old prayer. The Mishnah, in tractate Tamid, lists the words the priests said each morning in the Temple, and among them is emet v'yatziv. The Talmud even says that someone who didn't say emet v'yatziv in the morning, and its evening partner, emet ve'emunah, true and faithful, hasn't fulfilled their duty. Why so much insistence on one word? Because, in the prayer's order, hearing isn't the end. The Shema says hear. Then emet answers: I heard, and I hold it to be true. That's the word's job here: not only saying the words, but standing behind them.
screen: `THE LORD YOUR GOD IS TRUE.` · `NO PAUSE BETWEEN THEM.` · `WORD AFTER WORD, ALL SAYING YES.` · `SAID IN THE TEMPLE EACH MORNING.` · then, large: `TRUE AND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you hold to be true deep down, not an opinion about the news but something you'd stand behind, and say it to yourself in one sentence. Then, quietly, out loud, say: true. If doubt comes, let it come, and see what's still standing.
Emet v'Yatziv. True and firm: the blessing right after the morning Shema, answering what was heard with yes.
Your line: more than a dozen words, all saying yes. First you hear, then you stand behind it. That's day five hundred seventy.

571.title: Who is like you? (Exodus 15:11)
571.hook: the Song of the Sea returns: "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty?"
571.howItsDone: Mi Chamocha is part of the blessing after the Shema in the morning and evening services; in many synagogues the congregation sings it together, and the blessing then leads toward the standing prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emet v'Yatziv, the word true said right after the Shema. Your line was more than a dozen words, all saying yes. Today, that same blessing runs back to the sea.
screen: `MORE THAN A DOZEN WORDS, ALL SAYING YES.`

segments.voice: Twelve days ago, the Song of the Sea closed the verses of song. Since then: Barchu, the light, the angels, great love, the Shema and its three paragraphs, and the word true. You might think the sea was left behind. It isn't. As the blessing after the Shema builds, it tells the story of the rescue again, then quotes one line from that song, and in many synagogues everyone sings it together.
screen: `THE SEA, TWELVE DAYS AGO.` → `IT ISN'T LEFT BEHIND.` → `ONE LINE, SUNG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The line is from Exodus fifteen. In the old Jewish translation: "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty? Who is like unto Thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?" In Hebrew it begins mi chamocha, who is like you. The blessing sets it up as a scene: Moses and the people of Israel sang to you with great joy, and all of them said, mi chamocha. A little later it says the rescued sang a new song at the shore, and quotes the song's last line too: "The LORD shall reign for ever and ever." It's a question, but nobody's waiting for an answer. It's the kind you ask when you're amazed: who does that? The word translated mighty, elim, can also mean gods, and in the song's own world each nation had its gods; the song says none of them did what was done at the sea. There's a harder reading, too. A teaching in the Talmud, tractate Gittin, adds one letter and reads among the silent: who is like you, who sees suffering and keeps silent? It sits in the Talmud's account of the Temple's destruction, a reading born of grief. Both readings live in the tradition. And a later tradition says the Maccabees' name comes from the first letters of mi chamocha ba'elim Adonai. Others connect the name to a word for hammer, and the question is still debated. Every morning, though, the line is sung as it began: a question of wonder, from people standing on the far shore.

segments.voice: Think of something that amazed you lately, a kindness you didn't expect, a sunset, a child's sentence, and instead of describing it, ask it the way the song does: who does that? Let the question sit without an answer. If you pray, you can say mi chamocha ba'elim Adonai.
Mi Chamocha. Who is like you: the line from the Song of the Sea, sung in the blessing after the Shema.
Your line: a question of wonder. Who is like you, sung from the far shore. See you tomorrow.

572.title: No gap (Berakhot 4b)
572.hook: the Talmud says to join the blessing of redemption straight to the Amidah
572.howItsDone: In the morning and evening services, the last blessing after the Shema ends with ga'al Yisrael and the Amidah begins right away; the custom is to avoid any talking or pause between them, and in some synagogues the leader says the closing words quietly in the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mi Chamocha, the song from the far shore of the sea. Your line was a question of wonder. Today, the last step before the great prayer.

A knock at the door of a palace. The king hears it, gets up, crosses the long hall, and opens the door. Nobody there. The visitor knocked, then wandered off. The Jerusalem Talmud tells a parable close to this, about the king's friend who knocked and was gone by the time the door opened. It's a picture of a very specific mistake in prayer. You build up to the moment through the whole service, then, right at the threshold, you pause, chat, scroll, drift.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE PALACE DOOR.` → `THE DOOR OPENS. NOBODY THERE.` → `DON'T WANDER OFF AT THE THRESHOLD.`

segments.voice: The blessings after the Shema end on one theme: redemption. True and firm, the song at the sea, who is like you. The last blessing closes with the words ga'al Yisrael: blessed are You, who redeemed Israel. Then, immediately, the Amidah begins. In Berakhot 4b, Rabbi Yochanan asks who will inherit the world to come, and answers: the one who joins geulah, redemption, to tefillah, the prayer of the evening. Further on, in 9b, the Talmud adds that whoever joins redemption to prayer in the morning will come to no harm all that day. So the rule is: no gap. No chatting, no stepping out, between the last word about redemption and the first word of the Amidah. In some synagogues the leader even says ga'al Yisrael quietly in the morning, so the room doesn't pause to answer amen. Why does it matter so much? Geulah comes from a root that means to redeem, to buy back. A go'el in the Torah is the relative who buys back family land or a family member sold into debt. So the order of the service tells a story. First you remember being bought back, at the sea. Then, while that memory is still warm, you stand up and ask. Thanks flows straight into asking, the way someone just helped by a friend feels free to say: and one more thing.

segments.voice: Remember one time you were helped out of something, a bad week, a debt, a mess you couldn't fix alone, and let the relief come back. Then, without breaking the thread, move straight to one thing you need today, as a request if you pray or simply named to yourself. Keep the two touching, like the end of one sentence and the start of the next.
Geulah. Redemption, buying back. The theme the Shema's blessings end on, joined with no gap to the Amidah.
Your line: and one more thing. Remembering, then asking, with no gap between. Day five hundred seventy-two, done.

573.title: The standing prayer
573.hook: the central prayer, said standing, feet together, facing Jerusalem
573.howItsDone: Jews say the Amidah at the morning, afternoon and evening services, standing with feet together and facing toward Jerusalem; it's said silently by each person, and in a congregation with a minyan the leader then repeats it aloud at morning and afternoon services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, geulah, redemption, joined to prayer. Your line was and one more thing. Today, the prayer it runs into.

At one moment in every Jewish service, the room changes. Everyone stands. Feet come together. People turn, quietly, in the same direction. Lips move, but you hear almost nothing: a murmur, a page turning, someone's shoe. Some sway. Some stay perfectly still. For several minutes, a room full of people is completely silent and completely busy. This is the center of every Jewish service, morning, afternoon and evening, and its name just describes what the body is doing.
screen: `EVERYONE STANDS.` → `FEET TOGETHER, ONE DIRECTION.` → `A ROOM, SILENT AND BUSY.`

segments.voice: Amidah means standing. The Talmud often just calls it ha-tefillah, the prayer, as if there were no other. It's also called Shemoneh Esrei, eighteen, for its original eighteen blessings, though the weekday version now has nineteen. Over the coming weeks, they'll come one at a time. The posture is part of the prayer. Feet together: the Talmud, in Berakhot 10b, connects it to the angels in Ezekiel's vision, where it says "their feet were straight feet." One straight line, as if you had only one leg. Facing Jerusalem: when King Solomon dedicates the Temple, he asks God to hear people who pray toward their land, toward the city and the house. So in New York, people face east. In Jerusalem itself, they face the Temple Mount. A blind person, or someone who can't tell direction, the Talmud says, directs their heart instead. And it's said three times a day. Berakhot 26b gives two explanations: the patriarchs set them, Abraham the morning, Isaac the afternoon, Jacob the evening; or they stand in for the daily offerings of the Temple. Both answers are kept. Underneath it all, in the tradition's picture, the one praying is standing before someone. Not lounging, not walking past. Stopping, feet planted, facing one way, and for a few minutes nothing else gets the body.
screen: `AMIDAH: STANDING. HA-TEFILLAH.` · `FEET TOGETHER, LIKE THE ANGELS.` · `FACING JERUSALEM.` · `THREE TIMES A DAY.` · then, large: `STANDING BEFORE.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand up now, feet side by side, hands resting, facing one direction, and notice the small work your body does to stay upright. If you pray, let this be standing before God; if not, standing before the day. When the minute's up, sit, and keep breathing.
Amidah. Standing. The central prayer of every service, said on your feet, feet together, facing Jerusalem, three times a day.
Your line: standing before. Feet planted, facing one way, nothing else getting the body. Until tomorrow.

574.title: Three steps in
574.hook: many step back and then forward before beginning, as if approaching a king
574.howItsDone: Many Jews take three small steps forward before beginning the Amidah, often stepping back first to make room, and at the end take three steps back and bow to each side before stepping forward again; customs on the opening steps vary between communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Amidah, the prayer said on your feet. Your line was standing before. Today, what happens in the two seconds before the standing begins.

A pause in the doorway of a boss's office before you step in. People mark entrances even when nothing stands in the way. Before the Amidah, many Jews make one with their feet: three small steps backward, then three small steps forward, ending exactly where they started. If you didn't know, you'd think they'd forgotten something and changed their mind. But it's a whole entrance, compressed into six steps on a carpet, and it borrows its shape from the way people once walked into a throne room.
screen: `A PAUSE IN THE DOORWAY.` → `THREE BACK, THREE FORWARD.` → `AN ENTRANCE IN SIX STEPS.`

segments.voice: The steps forward are the older idea. Before you speak to a king, you approach. Commentators point to three moments in the Bible where someone draws near before speaking to God or to power. Abraham draws near to plead for Sodom. Judah draws near to Joseph, the ruler of Egypt, to plead for his brother. Elijah draws near on Mount Carmel before he prays. In the old Jewish translation, Genesis says simply: "And Abraham drew near." Three nearings, three steps. The step backward first is a later custom, and not everyone does it. The idea: you can't walk forward into a presence you're already standing in, so you make a little room, step back, and then come in properly. Halachic codes record the forward steps as a custom many keep. At the end of the Amidah there are three steps back again: the Talmud, in Yoma 53b, compares it to a student taking leave of a teacher, backing away rather than turning around. So the whole prayer sits inside a doorway: three steps in, three steps out. Prayer doesn't begin when the words begin. It begins when you decide to go in. Before the steps, you're in your day. After them, you're somewhere else, in front of someone. Same carpet. Different room.
screen: `APPROACH BEFORE YOU SPEAK.` · `ABRAHAM, JUDAH, ELIJAH DREW NEAR.` · `STEP BACK TO MAKE ROOM.` · `THREE STEPS IN, THREE STEPS OUT.` · then, large: `THREE STEPS IN.`

segments.voice: If you can stand, try it now: three small steps back, a pause, then three small steps forward; if not, take them in your mind. Stay where you've landed for a few breaths, and notice whether the same spot feels like a different room.
Drew near. Abraham, before pleading for Sodom; Judah, before Joseph; Elijah, before he prayed — the model for the three steps taken into the Amidah.

Your line: same carpet, different room. The week walked from the Shema's last paragraphs, through true and firm and the sea, to no gap, the standing prayer and its doorway. That's day five hundred seventy-four.
